lessons.title: Classic Smooth Peanut Butter Recipe
lessons.body:
To make classic smooth peanut butter, start with 1 kg of raw shelled peanuts. In Africa, groundnuts are common; use freshly shelled ones. Spread them on a baking tray and roast at 160Â°C for 20â25 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes, until golden brown and fragrant. If you don't have an oven, roast in a dry heavy pot over medium heat, stirring constantly for 10â15 minutes. Let cool for 10 minutes.

Next, remove skins. Rub peanuts between your palms or in a cloth; discard skins. You should have about 900 g after skinning. Put peanuts into a food processor or heavy-duty blender. Blend for 1 minute, scrape down sides, then blend again. Continue blending in 1-minute bursts until smooth â about 5â7 minutes total. The peanuts will first become crumbs, then a ball, then liquid. Add 1 teaspoon of salt and 1â2 tablespoons of peanut oil (or any neutral oil) to help the process. For a smoother texture, add up to 4 tablespoons of oil. Blend until completely smooth, about 2 more minutes.

If you want a pourable consistency, add another tablespoon of oil. Taste and adjust salt. For sweetness, add 1â2 teaspoons of sugar or honey, but classic smooth peanut butter often has no sweetener. Transfer to clean, dry glass jars. Press down to remove air bubbles. Seal tightly. Store in a cool, dark place for up to 3 months, or in the fridge for 6 months. Makes about 800 g.

For a local twist, use groundnut oil instead of neutral oil. In West Africa, many use a pinch of ground ginger or a small dried chili for subtle heat, but that's optional. Always sterilize jars by boiling for 10 minutes and drying. Label with date. This recipe is your base for all variations.

lessons.title: Crunchy Peanut Butter with Added Peanut Pieces
lessons.body:
Crunchy peanut butter is made exactly like smooth, but you reserve some chopped peanuts to add at the end. Start with 1 kg raw shelled peanuts. Roast at 160Â°C for 20â25 minutes, or in a dry pot for 10â15 minutes, stirring often. Cool, then skin. Set aside 200 g of the roasted peanuts. Chop these coarsely with a knife or pulse in a blender for 2â3 seconds â you want pieces about the size of rice grains. Do not over-blend into powder.

Take the remaining 800 g peanuts and make smooth peanut butter following the classic recipe: blend in a food processor for 5â7 minutes, adding 1 teaspoon salt and 2â4 tablespoons peanut oil until smooth. Once smooth, add the chopped peanuts and pulse 3â4 times just to mix. Do not blend long, or you'll lose the crunch. Taste and add salt if needed. You can also add 1 teaspoon of honey or sugar if you like a touch of sweetness, but it's optional.

Transfer to jars. Press down gently. The crunch will stay for months if sealed well. Makes about 800 g. For variation, use 150 g chopped peanuts for lighter crunch, or 250 g for extra crunch. In East Africa, some add roasted sesame seeds (50 g) for a different crunch. Store in a cool dark place for 3 months, or fridge for 6 months. Always label with date and 'crunchy'.

Note: If your blender struggles, do it in batches. Never add water â it causes mold. Use oil only. For a local flair, add a pinch of chili flakes or ground cinnamon to the chopped peanuts before mixing.

lessons.title: Spicy Peanut Butter with Chili and Local Spices
lessons.body:
Spicy peanut butter is a popular variation in many African markets. Start with 1 kg raw shelled peanuts. Roast and skin as in the classic recipe. In a dry pan, toast 2â4 dried red chilies (like bird's eye or cayenne) for 1 minute until fragrant, then remove seeds and crush. You can also use 1â2 teaspoons of chili powder. For local spices, gather 1 teaspoon ground ginger, 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon, and 1/4 teaspoon ground cloves or nutmeg. Some regions use ground dried shrimp or fish powder for umami, but that's optional.

Blend the 900 g skinned peanuts in a food processor for 5â7 minutes until smooth, adding 1 teaspoon salt and 2â4 tablespoons peanut oil. Once smooth, add the crushed chilies and spices. Blend for another 1â2 minutes to mix well. Taste â it should be spicy but balanced. Adjust chili to your preference. For a milder version, use 1 chili; for hot, use 4. You can also add 1 teaspoon of honey or sugar to round out the heat.

Transfer to jars. Store in a cool dark place for 3 months, or fridge for 6 months. Makes about 800 g. In West Africa, this is often called 'groundnut pepper soup' base. In Southern Africa, some add a pinch of smoked paprika. Always label with heat level. For a smoky flavor, roast the chilies with the peanuts for the last 5 minutes.

Safety: Wear gloves when handling chilies, and avoid touching your eyes. If you have sensitive skin, use powder instead. This spicy version is excellent on bread, in stews, or as a dip. Experiment with local spices like grains of paradise or African nutmeg.

lessons.title: Chocolate Peanut Butter: Using Cocoa Powder
lessons.body:
Chocolate peanut butter is a rich, popular product. Start with 1 kg raw shelled peanuts. Roast at 160Â°C for 20â25 minutes, or in a pot for 10â15 minutes, then cool and skin. You should have about 900 g. In a bowl, mix 4 tablespoons of unsweetened cocoa powder (not drinking chocolate) with 4 tablespoons of powdered sugar or honey. If using honey, warm it slightly for easier mixing. Set aside.

Blend the peanuts in a food processor for 5â7 minutes until smooth, adding 1 teaspoon salt and 2â4 tablespoons peanut oil. Once smooth, add the cocoa-sugar mixture. Blend for 2â3 minutes until fully incorporated. Taste â add more cocoa for darker chocolate, or more sugar for sweeter. For a milk chocolate style, add 2 tablespoons of powdered milk. For a darker, bitter version, reduce sugar to 2 tablespoons. You can also add a pinch of vanilla extract or ground vanilla bean.

Transfer to jars. Press down to remove air. Store in a cool dark place for 2 months (cocoa can go stale faster), or fridge for 4 months. Makes about 800 g. In Africa, local cocoa powder from Ghana or CÃ´te d'Ivoire is excellent. For a unique twist, add 1 teaspoon of ground coffee or a pinch of chili for a Mexican-style chocolate peanut butter.

Note: Cocoa powder absorbs oil, so you may need an extra tablespoon of oil. If the mixture is too thick, add oil slowly. Always label with date. This is great for gifts or value-added products. Experiment with local sweeteners like date syrup or jaggery.

lessons.title: Honey Peanut Butter: Using Local Honey
lessons.body:
Honey peanut butter uses local honey for natural sweetness and flavor. Start with 1 kg raw shelled peanuts. Roast and skin as usual. You should have about 900 g. In a small bowl, measure 4â6 tablespoons of raw local honey. If honey is thick, warm it gently in a bowl over hot water â do not boil, as it kills beneficial enzymes.

Blend the peanuts in a food processor for 5â7 minutes until smooth, adding 1 teaspoon salt and 2â3 tablespoons peanut oil. Once smooth, add the honey. Blend for 1â2 minutes until fully mixed. Taste â add more honey if you like it sweeter. For a runnier consistency, add another tablespoon of oil. For a thicker, spreadable butter, use less oil. You can also add 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon or a pinch of ground ginger for warmth.

Transfer to jars. Store in a cool dark place for 2 months, or fridge for 4 months. Honey can crystallize over time; if it does, place the jar in warm water to liquefy. Makes about 800 g. In Africa, honey from acacia, baobab, or miombo trees gives unique flavors. Always use pure honey, not syrup. Label with date and honey type.

Note: Honey peanut butter is more prone to separation; stir before use. For a vegan version, honey is not vegan, so use date syrup or maple syrup instead. This variation is excellent on pancakes, in smoothies, or as a dip for fruit. Experiment with local honey varieties for signature flavors.

lessons.title: Developing Your Own Signature Flavor
lessons.body:
Now that you've mastered the basics, it's time to create your own signature flavor. Start with a base of 1 kg roasted, skinned peanuts (about 900 g after skinning). Make smooth peanut butter using 1 teaspoon salt and 2â4 tablespoons peanut oil. This is your canvas. Think about local ingredients that tell your story: dried fruits like mango, banana, or baobab powder; spices like cloves, cardamom, or grains of paradise; or savory additions like dried tomato, onion powder, or ground dried fish.

Choose one main flavor and one accent. For example, 2 tablespoons of baobab powder for tang, plus 1 teaspoon of ground ginger. Or 3 tablespoons of dried mango powder, plus 1/2 teaspoon of chili. Add these after the peanut butter is smooth, then blend for 1â2 minutes. Taste and adjust. Keep notes: record exact amounts, roasting time, and oil used. This is your recipe development log. Make small batches first â 250 g peanuts â to avoid waste.

Consider texture: add 100 g chopped nuts, seeds, or dried fruit for crunch. Consider sweetness: honey, date syrup, or jaggery. Consider heat: chili, black pepper, or ginger. Consider umami: dried shrimp powder, soy sauce powder, or fermented locust bean (dawadawa). Balance is key â start with small amounts, taste, and add more. A signature flavor should be unique but not overpowering.

Once you have a winner, scale up to 1 kg batches. Test shelf life: store in a cool dark place and check after 1 week, 1 month, 3 months. If it separates, stir. If it molds, reduce moisture (avoid fresh ingredients). Package in clean jars with a label that includes your brand name, date, and ingredients. In Africa, unique flavors like moringa, hibiscus, or tamarind can set you apart. Sell at local markets, and ask for feedback. Adjust and refine. Your signature flavor is your business identity.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Product Development and Flavour Variations for Peanut Butter & Nut Pastes

This practical reference is written for African agribusinesses â from smallholder cooperatives in Malawi and Senegal to urban food processors in Kenya, Ghana and Nigeria â that want to move beyond a single commodity paste into a portfolio of differentiated, higher-margin products. Flavour variation is not a gimmick: it is a pricing strategy. A plain 250 g jar of peanut butter may sell for the equivalent of US$1.50â2.50, while a branded chocolate or honey variant in attractive packaging can command 30â80% more in supermarkets and export markets. This module gives you the technical parameters, safety boundaries and commercial logic to develop six core products and then design your own signature flavour.

1. The Base Process, Visualised

2. Six Core Products: Formulation and Positioning

The table below gives working formulation ranges for each of the six lessons in this module. Percentages are by weight of the finished product and should be adjusted to local taste panels. "Positioning" is the commercial rationale â what the product is for, and who pays for it.

Table 1: Indicative formulations and commercial positioning for six peanut butter variants
Product Key ingredients (% w/w) Process note Positioning / margin logic
Classic Smooth Roasted peanuts 90â95%; salt 0.5â1%; stabiliser (palm oil or groundnut oil) 2â5%; sugar 0â3% Grind to 20â30 Âµm particle size; single or double pass colloid mill Volume anchor product. Lowest cost, highest turnover. Builds brand trust.
Crunchy with Peanut Pieces Smooth base 80â88%; chopped roasted peanuts 12â20% (3â5 mm pieces) Fold pieces in after grinding; avoid over-mixing to prevent paste discolouration Premium 10â20% over smooth. Appeals to adult and export markets.
Spicy with Chili & Local Spices Base 88â94%; dried chili 1â3%; ginger/garlic powder 1â2%; smoked paprika 0.5â1%; salt adjusted Add spices as a pre-blended slurry with 1â2% oil for even dispersion Differentiated snack/culinary product. Strong in urban informal retail and food service.
Chocolate Peanut Butter Base 78â85%; cocoa powder 5â10%; sugar 5â10%; optional cocoa butter 1â2% Use alkalised (Dutched) cocoa for darker colour and milder taste; mix at 35â40 Â°C Highest margin in the range. Targets children, bakery and gifting segments.
Honey Peanut Butter Base 82â90%; local honey 8â15%; salt reduced to 0.3â0.5% Add honey at < 45 Â°C to preserve enzymes and aroma; expect slight crystallisation over time Health-and-origin story. Premium 25â40%. Sells well in tourist and diaspora markets.
Signature Flavour Base 80â92%; 1â3 flavour components (e.g. baobab, moringa, coconut, vanilla, coffee) Run 3â5 pilot batches; conduct blind taste test with 20â30 target consumers Brand-defining SKU. Protects against price competition and copycats.

Sources: formulation ranges compiled from FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius CXS 192-1995 (General Standard for Food Additives), ICRISAT (2019) Groundnut Production and Processing Manual, and published small-scale peanut butter processing guides from the Peanut Collaborative Research Support Program (Peanut CRSP). Adjust to your national standards authority requirements.

3. Quality, Shelf Life and Costing Parameters

Flavour variants fail commercially for two reasons: they separate or go rancid before the sell-by date, or they are priced above what the local market will bear. Table 2 gives the operating parameters that determine both.

Table 2: Quality, shelf-life and costing parameters for flavoured nut pastes
Parameter Target / range Why it matters commercially
Moisture content < 2% for plain; < 4% for honey variants Above these levels, mould risk rises and shelf life collapses. Honey adds water â compensate with a tighter base.
Water activity (aw) < 0.6 Below 0.6, most spoilage bacteria and moulds cannot grow. Critical for ambient tropical storage.
Aflatoxin (total) < 10 Âµg/kg (Codex); < 4 Âµg/kg for EU export Non-negotiable for export. One rejected container can end a contract and damage a cooperative's reputation.
Peroxide value (rancidity) < 10 meq O2/kg at end of shelf life Determines whether the product still tastes good at month 9. Add natural antioxidants (tocopherols) or nitrogen flush.
Shelf life (ambient, 25â30 Â°C) 6â9 months plain; 4â6 months for cocoa and honey variants Set your sell-by date from real stability trials, not optimism. Shorter dates on premium SKUs are acceptable if the price reflects freshness.
Packaging Glass or PET jars with induction seal; sachets for single-serve Glass signals premium; sachets open the low-income, high-frequency market. Match pack to channel.
Ingredient cost share Peanuts 55â70% of variable cost Flavour ingredients are usually < 15% of cost but can justify 30â80% price uplift â this is the margin engine.
Break-even volume (illustrative) 1,500â3,000 jars/month for a micro-processor Below this, fixed costs (labour, rent, certification) eat the margin. Plan flavour launches around existing volume.

Sources: Codex Alimentarius CXS 193-1995 (General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed); FAO (2004) Good Practices for the Prevention and Reduction of Aflatoxin in Groundnuts; ICRISAT (2019); and industry costing benchmarks from the African Agricultural Transformation Scorecard and AGRA agribusiness reports.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Aflatoxin and Allergen Control

Groundnuts are highly susceptible to Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus moulds, which produce aflatoxins â carcinogenic compounds that are not destroyed by normal roasting or grinding. Never use discoloured, mouldy, shrivelled or insect-damaged nuts. Reject any lot that tests above 10 Âµg/kg total aflatoxin (4 Âµg/kg for export to the EU). Store raw nuts below 10% moisture and at < 25 Â°C with good ventilation. Roasting at 150â180 Â°C reduces but does not eliminate aflatoxin â prevention at farm and storage level is the only reliable control. Separately, peanut is a major allergen: declare "contains peanuts" on every label, use dedicated equipment, and never repack a non-peanut product on the same line without full clean-down. Failure on either point can cause illness, death or market exclusion.

4. Developing Your Own Signature Flavour

A signature flavour is the fastest route from commodity supplier to brand. The discipline is to work in small, documented batches and to test with real buyers before investing in packaging. A practical sequence:

  1. Choose a local, story-rich ingredient. Baobab (Malawi, Senegal, Zimbabwe), moringa (Kenya, Ghana), coconut (Mozambique, Tanzania), hibiscus (Nigeria, Sudan), coffee (Ethiopia, Uganda, Rwanda), vanilla (Madagascar, Uganda) or local chili varieties all carry origin value that imported flavours cannot.
  2. Fix the base first. Get a smooth, stable 90% peanut base that does not separate. Only then add the flavour component at 2â10%.
  3. Run 3â5 pilot batches at 2 kg each, varying the flavour level. Record temperature, mixing time and particle size.
  4. Blind taste test with 20â30 target consumers â not staff. Score for taste, texture, aroma and purchase intent at a stated price.
  5. Check regulatory fit. Confirm the ingredient is permitted, that you can declare it correctly, and that any health claim you make is allowed by your national standards authority.
  6. Cost and price it. Target a gross margin of at least 35â45% on premium SKUs. If the flavour ingredient pushes cost above that, reduce the level or raise the pack price.
  7. Protect it. Register the brand name and, where possible, the recipe trade secret. A signature flavour is intellectual property.

5. Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Raw nuts screened for mould, discolouration and insect damage; aflatoxin tested before processing.
  • â Roasting profile recorded (temperature and time) and repeated batch to batch for consistent flavour.
  • â Base paste ground to a stable, non-separating consistency before any flavour is added.
  • â Flavour ingredients measured by weight, not volume, and pre-blended for even dispersion.
  • â Moisture and water activity checked; honey and cocoa variants adjusted for added water.
  • â Shelf-life trial run for at least 8 weeks at ambient temperature before setting a sell-by date.
  • â Allergen declaration ("contains peanuts") and ingredient list on every label, in the local language.
  • â Unit cost, pack price and gross margin calculated per SKU before launch; break-even volume known.

6. Further Reading

  • FAO â Fruit and Vegetable Processing (processing principles applicable to nut pastes)
  • FAO â Good Practices for the Prevention and Reduction of Aflatoxin in Groundnuts
  • FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius â General Standards for Contaminants and Food Additives (CXS 192-1995, CXS 193-1995)
  • ICRISAT â Groundnut post-harvest and processing resources
  • AGRA â Agribusiness and value-addition reports for African processors

Prepared for the RISE AFRICA Skills programme â Peanut Butter & Nut Pastes, Module: Product Development and Flavor Variations. Adapt all figures to your national regulatory requirements and local market conditions.

quiz.q: What is the recommended roasting temperature for peanuts in an oven?
quiz.explanation: Roasting at 160Â°C for 20â25 minutes gives golden brown, fragrant peanuts without burning.

quiz.q: How much salt is typically added to 1 kg of peanuts for classic smooth peanut butter?
quiz.explanation: The recipe uses 1 teaspoon of salt for 1 kg of peanuts.

quiz.q: What oil is commonly used in Africa for peanut butter?
quiz.explanation: Groundnut oil is locally available and commonly used in African peanut butter.

quiz.q: How long should you blend peanuts in a food processor to get smooth butter?
quiz.explanation: Blending for 5â7 minutes in bursts yields a smooth consistency.

quiz.q: What is the shelf life of classic smooth peanut butter in a cool dark place?
quiz.explanation: Properly stored classic peanut butter lasts about 3 months in a cool dark place.

quiz.q: For crunchy peanut butter, how much of the roasted peanuts are set aside for chopping?
quiz.explanation: The recipe reserves 200 g of roasted peanuts to chop for crunch.

quiz.q: What size should the chopped peanut pieces be for crunchy peanut butter?
quiz.explanation: Chopping to about rice grain size gives a pleasant crunch without being too large.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid adding water to peanut butter?
options: A) It makes it too thin
D) It adds too much sweetness
quiz.explanation: Water introduces moisture that can lead to mold growth.

quiz.q: Which local spice is suggested for spicy peanut butter?
quiz.explanation: The recipe suggests ground ginger, cinnamon, and cloves as local spices.

quiz.q: How many dried red chilies are recommended for a hot spicy peanut butter?
quiz.explanation: Using 4 chilies gives a hot version; adjust to taste.

quiz.q: What should you wear when handling chilies?
quiz.explanation: Gloves protect your skin from chili oils and prevent irritation.

quiz.q: What type of cocoa powder should be used for chocolate peanut butter?
quiz.explanation: Unsweetened cocoa powder gives pure chocolate flavor without added sugar.

quiz.q: How much cocoa powder is suggested for 1 kg of peanuts in chocolate peanut butter?
quiz.explanation: The recipe uses 4 tablespoons of unsweetened cocoa powder.

quiz.q: What can be added to make a milk chocolate style peanut butter?
quiz.explanation: Powdered milk adds a creamy, milk chocolate flavor.

quiz.q: How does cocoa powder affect the oil content in peanut butter?
options: B) It absorbs oil, so you may need more
quiz.explanation: Cocoa powder absorbs oil, so an extra tablespoon may be needed.

quiz.q: What is the shelf life of chocolate peanut butter in a cool dark place?
quiz.explanation: Cocoa can go stale faster, so store for up to 2 months in a cool dark place.

quiz.q: How much honey is suggested for honey peanut butter?
quiz.explanation: The recipe uses 4â6 tablespoons of honey for 1 kg of peanuts.

quiz.q: What should you do if honey crystallizes in the jar?
options: C) Warm the jar in warm water
quiz.explanation: Warming the jar in warm water liquefies crystallized honey without damaging it.

quiz.q: Which honey type is mentioned as giving unique flavors in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Acacia, baobab, and miombo honeys are all mentioned for unique flavors.

quiz.q: What can be used instead of honey for a vegan version?
quiz.explanation: Date syrup or maple syrup are vegan alternatives to honey.

quiz.q: What is the first step in developing a signature flavor?
options: B) Start with a base of smooth peanut butter
quiz.explanation: Start with a base of smooth peanut butter made from 1 kg roasted peanuts.

quiz.q: Why should you make small batches when experimenting?
quiz.explanation: Small batches prevent wasting ingredients if the flavor doesn't work.

quiz.q: Which of these is a suggested local ingredient for signature flavors?
quiz.explanation: Baobab powder, dried mango, and ground dried fish are all suggested.

quiz.q: What should you record in your recipe development log?
quiz.explanation: Record exact amounts, roasting time, and oil used for consistency.

quiz.q: What is a good way to test shelf life of your signature flavor?
options: B) Store and check after 1 week, 1 month, 3 months
quiz.explanation: Checking at intervals helps determine safe shelf life without preservatives.

quiz.q: What should you avoid adding to prevent mold in peanut butter?
options: C) Fresh ingredients with high moisture
quiz.explanation: Fresh ingredients with high moisture can introduce mold.

quiz.q: Which of these is a suggested unique African flavor for peanut butter?
quiz.explanation: Moringa, hibiscus, and tamarind are all mentioned as unique flavors.

quiz.q: What is the recommended jar sterilization method?
options: B) Boil for 10 minutes and dry
quiz.explanation: Boiling jars for 10 minutes and drying them sterilizes them for safe storage.

quiz.q: How much peanut oil is typically added to 1 kg of peanuts for smooth peanut butter?
quiz.explanation: The recipe uses 2â4 tablespoons of peanut oil to help blending.

quiz.q: What is a key step after blending peanut butter before jarring?
quiz.explanation: Tasting and adjusting salt ensures the flavor is right before packaging.
